Description Title: Repeated Behavior Score Drops Over an Extended Period Despite Positive Match History Hello Dota 2 Team, I am reporting a recurring issue with my Behavior Score and Communication Score that has been frustrating me for a long time. This is not an isolated incident. For an extended period, I have repeatedly experienced the same pattern: my scores increase after playing matches, but when the next 15-match summary is updated, they drop again. This cycle has happened multiple times, making it extremely difficult for me to maintain a score above the 3000 threshold required to access ranked matchmaking. After my latest 15 matches, my Behavior Score dropped from 3058 to 2953, a decrease of 105 points. My latest match summary shows: - 13 positive matches out of 15 - 29 Commends received - 0 abandoned matches - 0 Communication Reports - Excessive Reports: No - 2 reported matches I consistently try to play fairly and positively, often receive MVP awards, and receive numerous Commends. Despite this, my scores repeatedly fluctuate, and I keep losing access to ranked matchmaking. I understand that Commends and positive matches do not guarantee an increase in Behavior Score. However, the repeated nature of these drops over an extended period makes me concerned that there may be an issue with the scoring system or how my account's scores are being calculated. Could you please investigate this recurring issue or clarify what could be causing these repeated decreases? I can provide screenshots of my previous scores, updated scores, and match summaries as evidence. Thank you for your time and consideration. ### Example Match ID (and possibly Timestamp) _No response_ ### Screenshots Description Hello Valve developers, I would like to report a possible issue with the Behavior Score and Overwatch systems in Dota 2. On October 14, 2026, I received a 24-hour matchmaking ban with a notification stating that Overwatch had found me guilty of a gameplay violation. At the same time, my Behavior Score dropped from 2,215 to 1,465. However, my latest conduct summary shows the following statistics: - 15 matches played - 14 positive matches - Only 1 report - 39 commends - 0 abandoned matches - 0 communication reports - Excessive Reports: Yes I find this particularly confusing because the system marked my account as having excessive reports despite showing only one report in the latest summary. Recently, I have been playing Turbo matches to practice Invoker. I deliberately chose Turbo because I am still learning the hero and do not want to negatively affect other players in ranked or regular All Pick matches. I have not intentionally fed, griefed, or attempted to ruin anyone's games. I have simply been practicing a difficult hero while trying my best to win. I understand that making mistakes while learning a hero is normal, but I do not believe that poor performance alone should be treated as intentional griefing. I kindly ask the developers to investigate the following: 1. Why did my Behavior Score decrease despite having only one report and 39 commends? 2. Why was my account flagged with "Excessive Reports: Yes"? 3. Was the Overwatch punishment correctly applied? 4. Is there a possible issue affecting players with already low Behavior Scores? If this punishment was issued incorrectly, I would appreciate a review and restoration of the Behavior Score points that were unfairly deducted. I have attached a screenshot of my conduct summary as supporting evidence. Thank you for your time and attention. ### Example Match ID (and possibly Timestamp) 9044490273 ### Screenshots _No ### Description Additional evidence: Rapid Communication Score decrease Hello, I would like to add a documented case of a rapid Communication Score decrease to this discussion. Account ID: 114342752 Observed score changes * My Behavior Score remained close to the maximum of 12,000. * My Communication Score dropped from 12,000 to approximately 7,300 within seven days — a decrease of roughly 4,700 points. * For approximately a year before this period, my Communication Score fluctuations had generally been no more than around 500 points. * My communication features were temporarily restored when my score was approximately 8,200, but the score subsequently dropped again to 7,382. Conduct Summary evidence My documented Conduct Summary includes: * 0 abandons across the reviewed periods * 285 matches in the previously reviewed data * 692 commendations * 32 total reports and 26 Communication Reports in that earlier dataset * In the latest visible 15-match period: 14 positive matches, 1 reported match, 3 total reports, 9 Communication Reports from 7 reporting parties, and a Behavior Score of 11,997 The latest figures are from a newer period and should be considered separately from the earlier totals. Why I am reporting this I understand that Behavior Score and Communication Score are separate automated systems, and I am not claiming that these numbers alone prove a bug. However, the speed and magnitude of this decrease are substantially different from my previous score history. I would like to know whether this could be caused by an issue with Communication Report processing or score calculation. I really don’t get why there is a mechanic like this, it’s basically meant to be for griefers… why is everyone allowed to decrease your score and why we don’t have the Overwatch system for this too. It does not make any sense and ruins the game for me. I play the game since 2013 and even before, but that’s the official start, I never ever was not able to communicate with my team in 13 years, but now suddenly in 1 week i lose half of my communication rights? Honestly this does noch fit and does not make any sense at all. Since I am grown up now and I am not toxic at all… Could the Dota 2 team clarify whether this behavior is expected and whether there is a way to verify that reports contributing to a Communication Score were processed correctly? Description I am filing this report to formally contest three consecutive Overwatch convictions that came from human reviewers, not from any automated flag, issued under the griefing category, commonly referred to as trolling, which is the only category that could conceivably apply to what happened in my games. None of these convictions match what I actually did. I stayed for the full duration of each match, played my role, did not feed, did not abuse abilities against my own team, did not script, and did not troll in any sense of the word. These three convictions cover four match numbers, since I have no way of knowing for certain which of two specific matches triggered the third one. The first conviction corresponds to match 9005713707, played on September 19, 2026. The second corresponds to match 9008919256, played on September 20, 2026. For the third, I am attaching both candidate matches, 9011897482 and 9011927420, played on September 22, 2026 an hour apart. In all four matches there were teammates or opponents who evidently did not like the way I played. I stayed for the full duration in all four, and in none of them did the team's loss depend on me; when the team won, on the other hand, it won partly thanks to my cooperation. I am attaching screenshots from each of these four matches showing full attendance along with performance statistics that are consistent with normal, competitive play and inconsistent with griefing. I am also prepared to provide the replay files if that would help a human reviewer, Valve employee, or anyone with the authority to look at this case directly. I want to note that I have personally reviewed hundreds of Overwatch cases as a community reviewer, deciding each time whether the reported behavior actually amounted to griefing. That experience is exactly why these three verdicts are difficult to reconcile: the standard I apply when reviewing other players' matches does not match the standard that was apparently applied to mine. And this is not an isolated problem limited to my case: any player can report another simply because something personally annoyed them, without that implying an actual violation. Someone can report a teammate for trolling because they stole a last hit on a creep, or because that player did not play the way they personally would have liked, and that report reaches review with the same weight as a report over an actual violation. That is why any serious review of these cases should rest on a clear and strict rule: what gets sanctioned has to be universally sanctionable, not something that is only sanctionable according to the judgment of whoever filed the report or whoever reviewed that particular case. Universally sanctionable means that, in any possible context and under any reasonable interpretation, that way of playing is evidently trolling, not a forced reading of a normal play. Intentionally getting yourself killed falls into that category. Persistently stealing farm from the hard carry, ignoring roles and with no tactical reason, also falls into it. Clearly and consistently not respecting your role, for example staying in the jungle for forty minutes without leaving, whether you are the hard carry or a support, is also universally sanctionable. What does not fall into that category is, for example, a support not itemizing the way another player thinks they should, because the build in each match depends on how that specific match unfolds and is not a fixed standard. Reports like that should not even reach the review stage, let alone turn into a conviction. On top of that, there is no channel through which Steam Support can manually review, at the request of the sanctioned player, the exact moment of the match that was reported for trolling. The convicted player is given no timestamp, no description of the reported action, and no explanation of what led a reviewer to a guilty verdict, and there is no way to ask anyone to look at that specific moment again. Three consecutive convictions under those conditions, with no way to see the reasoning behind them and no way to ask for them to be reconsidered, amount to a punitive system with no accountability toward the people it judges. I am not claiming every Overwatch verdict is wrong. My complaint is specific: whoever reviewed these three cases did not apply any universally sanctionable standard, and having reviewed hundreds of cases myself, I know what that standard looks like in practice. If the same account received three wrong convictions in a row, whatever led reviewers to reach that verdict deserves scrutiny on its own, independent of whether any single case would have been overturned on individual appeal. I am formally requesting a manual review of the matches mentioned above by Valve, carried out by someone with direct access to the original reports, the reviewer decisions, and the full replays of the three convictions, with specific access to the exact moment reported in each case, and with the outcome communicated back to me directly rather than left as a silent score adjustment. Every piece of evidence I have access to as a player is included here or available on request. What I am asking for is a genuine review of the three cases that led to this point, under a standard that clearly distinguishes real trolling from a play that someone simply did not like. ### Example Description Hello Valve / Dota 2 Team, I am reporting a problem with the current Overwatch and behavior restriction system and, more specifically, the lack of transparency or an appeal/review mechanism for players who receive an Overwatch conviction. I have been playing Dota 2 since November 4, 2012, and this account has been part of my gaming history for almost 14 years. Recently, my Behavior Score dropped from 7,987 to 3,077 in a relatively short period of time. During this period I received multiple Low Priority penalties, and my communication features were eventually disabled. The most recent penalty was particularly concerning because it was issued after an Overwatch review. The match in question is: Match ID: 9001535070 Hero: Outworld Destroyer Result: Victory Score: 23 / 4 / 15 MVP Reports: 2 Commends: 28 After contacting Steam Support, I specifically asked them to investigate what happened to my account or, if Steam Support could not investigate Overwatch decisions, to provide me with a way to contact the team responsible for reviewing them. Steam Support confirmed that the matchmaking restriction was caused by an Overwatch conviction and later confirmed that the conviction was based on this exact match (9001535070). However, Steam Support also told me that: - they do not review or remove Overwatch restrictions; - they cannot provide contact information for the Overwatch team; - and there is no alternative appeal channel they can provide. I understand that Steam Support may not have the ability to manually remove an Overwatch restriction. I am not asking for special treatment or for Valve to simply remove my penalty because I disagree with it. My concern is the lack of transparency. If an Overwatch conviction is based on a specific match, I believe the affected player should at least be able to understand what behavior was considered a violation. At the moment, I have no information about: 1. What specific behavior in match 9001535070 resulted in the conviction. 2. What category of violation was identified. 3. What part or timestamp of the replay was considered evidence. 4. Whether the conviction was reviewed by multiple reviewers or how the verdict was validated. 5. Whether there is any mechanism to challenge an incorrect Overwatch verdict. I fully understand that a good KDA, winning a match, or receiving MVP does not automatically prove that no violation occurred. I am therefore not claiming that my statistics alone prove the conviction was wrong. The problem is that I have no way to determine what I supposedly did wrong in the first place. This is especially concerning because the affected player cannot meaningfully learn from or challenge a decision when the only information provided is that an Overwatch conviction occurred. There is also an important context regarding my recent Behavior Score history. Between two of my recent conduct summaries, my Behavior Score changed from 3,902 to 3,077. During those seven matches I won 6 out of 7 games. The final match in that sequence was the Outworld Destroyer game mentioned above, which was a 23/4/15 victory with 28 commends and 2 reports. Again, I am not presenting this as proof that the Overwatch verdict must be wrong. I am providing it because the circumstances make it particularly important for me to understand what behavior was actually reviewed and why it resulted in a conviction. I am also a long-time Dota 2 streamer and content creator. Because I regularly stream my games, I have experienced situations where viewers or other players intentionally watch the stream and interact with the game around it. I cannot prove that this caused the reports or the Overwatch conviction, so I am not presenting it as a fact. However, I believe it is a relevant possibility when investigating unusual reporting patterns on a streaming account. I am not asking Valve to reveal the identities of Overwatch reviewers or any private information about them. I am asking for a reasonable way for an affected player to understand and, when appropriate, challenge an Overwatch decision. My questions to the Dota 2 team are therefore: - Is there currently any way for a player to obtain information about the specific violation that resulted in an Overwatch conviction? - Is there any mechanism for reviewing or appealing a potentially incorrect Overwatch verdict? - How does Valve ensure that Overwatch convictions are sufficiently validated before they result in matchmaking restrictions and major Behavior Score penalties? - If a conviction is found to be incorrect, is there any mechanism to correct the resulting Behavior Score or other penalties? I have been playing Dota 2 for almost 14 years and I genuinely do not want to leave the game because of a punishment that I cannot understand or challenge. I would appreciate it if the Dota 2 team could clarify how this system is intended to work from the perspective of the player receiving the conviction. Description Dota 2 progressively loses performance during a single client session. FPS decreases both within an individual match and across consecutive matches while the same Dota 2 process remains running. I found a reproducible workaround: blocking dota2.com through the Windows hosts file almost completely prevents the progressive FPS degradation. The entry is: `0.0.0.0 dota2.com` This does not block the actual game servers. Matchmaking and normal matches continued to work during my tests. System configuration CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700 GPU: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT 16 GB RAM: 32 GB DDR5 OS: Windows 11 Pro Resolution: 2560 × 1440 Refresh rate: 320 Hz Rendering API: Vulkan Changing graphics settings has very little effect on the degradation pattern, so this does not appear to be a normal GPU bottleneck. ### Behavior without blocking dota2.com After a fresh launch of Dota 2: First match: start: approximately 300–310 FPS; after around 15 minutes: 200–220 FPS; end of the match: approximately 185–190 FPS. If the client is not restarted, the next match already starts at a significantly lower performance level. Second match: start: approximately 200–210 FPS; end: around 160 FPS. The following match may start at only around 180 FPS. If I continue playing using the same Dota 2 process, performance eventually degrades to approximately 100–110 FPS. In other words, each subsequent match appears to inherit part of the performance loss from the previous one. ### A/B test with dota2.com I repeated the test after adding the following line to the Windows hosts file: `0.0.0.0 dota2.com` I then ran: `ipconfig /flushdns` and fully restarted Dota 2. I played three consecutive matches without restarting the client between them. The result was significantly different: the progressive degradation was almost completely gone. Even after three consecutive matches, average FPS remained around 300. The behavior can be summarized approximately as: Normal: Match 1: ~310 → ~190 FPS Match 2: ~210 → ~160 FPS Match 3+: starts progressively lower Long session: ~100–110 FPS possible dota2.com blocked: Match 1: ~300 FPS Match 2: ~300 FPS Match 3: ~300 FPS Absolute FPS naturally varies depending on what is happening in the match, but the progressive loss between matches is almost completely absent when the domain is blocked. ### Network observations I also captured Dota 2 traffic with Wireshark. The client regularly connects to: `dota2.com` It also uses: `cdn.dota2.com` including for Dota React assets and video content. However, the workaround described above blocks only: `dota2.com` `cdn.dota2.com` was not blocked during this test. This does not prove the exact root cause, but it provides a reproducible way to significantly change the behavior of the problem. It may be worth investigating web/dashboard/Panorama content associated with dota2.com for resource accumulation or background work that persists during long client sessions. ### Additional observation The command: `map_enable_portrait_worlds 0` also produces a noticeable performance improvement. However, it is not a usable workaround because it breaks Dark Carnival and other UI elements that depend on background worlds. This may be related, but I have not confirmed a direct connection. ### Steps to reproduce Fully close and freshly launch Dota 2. Keep graphics settings, resolution and FPS limit unchanged. Play several normal matches consecutively without restarting Dota. Compare FPS at the beginning and end of each match. Observe that subsequent matches begin at progressively lower FPS. Close Dota 2. Add the following entry to the Windows hosts file: 0.0.0.0 dota2.com Run: ipconfig /flushdns Launch Dota 2 again. Play another three consecutive matches. Compare the FPS degradation between the two tests. On my system, the second test almost completely prevents the progressive FPS degradation. ### Expected behavior With unchanged settings and comparable scene complexity, performance should not continuously decrease simply because several matches have been played using the same Dota 2 process. Ending a match should release or reset resources that could otherwise reduce the performance of the following match. ### Actual behavior Without blocking dota2.com, FPS progressively decreases during a match and continues to deteriorate across subsequent matches. With dota2.com blocked, this cumulative degradation is almost completely absent, and performance remains close to its initial level even after three consecutive matches. ### Workaround side effects Blocking dota2.com affects Dota's web content. Some news, patch notes, videos, or other dashboard content may no longer load. For that reason, I am not suggesting this as a proper fix. I am reporting it as a diagnostic observation that may help identify the underlying issue. ### Related issues This appears related to: #35002 — Progressive FPS degradation across consecutive matches #35311 — Severe FPS degradation during a match / very low GPU utilization This report adds the observation that blocking dota2.com almost completely prevents the degradation on my system. ### The backend forces a double penalty for a single batch of reports because it fails to flag processed report rows as closed. ### 3-Year Accumulation Loop (~2,600 matches total) My attached chart shows that my **Chat Reports are at absolute ZERO** due to a system mute. Yet, these broken `Periodic: No` rows keep dragging both my Behavior and Comms scores into the dirt. Over 2,700 matches, this loop has silently stolen several thousand points from my profile, locking it below the 5k line with zero mathematical way to recover. Please fix the script responsible for injecting `Periodic: No` updates so it stops re-evaluating already processed reports. ### 🛠️ Proposed 3-Step Behavior System Reform To completely resolve the database overflow and prevent players from falling into mathematical limbo, Valve needs to implement these three structural fixes: 1. **Global Amnesty Reset:** Reset all active player accounts to a baseline of 12,000 Behavior/Communication points. This is necessary to completely clear existing database overflows, bugged logs, and duplicated report rows across the board. 2. **Decouple Behavior from Communication:** Completely separate the Communication Score logic from the Gameplay Behavior Score. A communication lock or an automated mute must never degrade matchmaking parameters or general behavior metrics. 3. **Finite Reporting Resources (Action Tokens):** Convert the current infinite reporting tools into a strictly finite system (e.g., Action Tokens, similar to Role Queue tokens). Description Hello Valve / Dota 2 Team, I enjoy Dota and play it whenever I have free time. However, for several years now, I have been stuck in what feels like a nightmare of this game, with a Behavior Score fluctuating between 0 and 5,000. Since I don't play Ranked, I don't have the option to avoid parties. As many players know, party players tend to report solo players, shifting the blame for their own poor performance onto the one player who isn't in their group. This happens very often. Currently, I can't even reach 3,000 Behavior Score. It feels like the system intentionally places me in matches right when I'm about to hit that mark, matching me with a full party of four players — which means four reports. This leads me straight into Overwatch. And Overwatch, as it stands, almost always returns a guilty verdict. There are discussions where people admit they click "Guilty" on every case without reviewing the replay at all. As a result, you lose 1,000 points from the verdict, and the reports also throw you into Low Priority games, where you continue to get reported endlessly. In total, you lose around 1,500 points, and you're back to 1,000 Behavior Score. The cycle repeats endlessly, and there is simply no way out of it in the current state of the system. I see many other players reporting similar issues on your GitHub. About two months ago, I finally became so frustrated that I took a break after receiving 4 Low Priority games. I returned recently for the event and noticed that matchmaking had been reworked — I hoped the Behavior Score system had received some attention as well. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case. I struggled through those Low Priority games, managed to play 4 All Pick matches, and then received another punishment from Overwatch. In all 4 of those games, I was the only solo player on my team. There were constant pings directed at me, insults, and likely reports as well. I played well in all of those matches, and there was absolutely no valid reason for a penalty. I realize that nobody is going to review these games, but to support my claim, here is the Match ID from which I received the punishment: 8956143152. By the way, in that same match, the Terrorblade player destroys his items at 48:18. But naturally, no one will report him because he is playing with his friends in a party and can do whatever he wants — they are just having fun. I believe there are several ways to improve this system and potentially bring back hundreds, or even thousands, of players who have left because of these issues. For example: 1. Introduce a "Behavior Score Reset Token" as a reward in one of the events, at least once a year — for instance, in the Quartero's Curios event at level 150. This token would be non-tradable, non-giftable, and usable only once per account, setting the Behavior Score to its maximum value. Ruiners would drop back down in just a few games anyway, so this wouldn't harm normal players in any way. 2. Extend the "Avoid Party" feature to unranked matches, just as it already exists in Ranked. This would at least partially prevent situations where a solo player receives 4 reports and ends up in Overwatch, leading to automatic Low Priority games. 3. Increase the accountability and quality standards for Overwatch reviewers. Currently, there is no penalty for reviewers who hand out "Guilty" verdicts without properly reviewing the evidence. Implementing a quality check or a verification mechanism for Overwatch cases would ensure that only genuine griefers are punished, and innocent players are not caught in a faulty automated loop. I see many posts here about the flaws in the Behavior Score system, and I truly hope you take this feedback into consideration. Thank you for your time and for this incredible Dota 2 developers and community, I would like to ask for clarification regarding the current Behavior Score and Communication Score system. My current scores are: Behavior Score: 12,000 / 12,000 (maximum) Communication Score: 5,800 / 12,000 I regularly play Dota 2 and I do not intentionally grief, feed, destroy my items, abandon matches, throw games, or smurf. In ranked games, I play the roles assigned to me by the matchmaking system and try to play for the win. I also support Dota 2 financially and enjoy the game, which is why I would like to understand how this system works and how it could potentially be improved. I recently checked my Steam Personal Game Data → Dota 2 → Account → Incoming Match Player Report. My recent data shows Communication Reports even during periods where I had no abandons or excessive reports. For example: August 11: - 15 matches - 15 positive matches - 0 reported matches - 0 abandons - 3 Communication Reports from 2 reporting parties August 8: - 15 matches - 14 positive matches - 1 reported match - 0 abandons - 4 Communication Reports from 3 reporting parties August 6: - 15 matches - 11 positive matches - 4 reported matches - 0 abandons - 7 total reports - 4 Communication Reports from 4 reporting parties August 2: - 15 matches - 15 positive matches - 0 reported matches - 0 abandons - 0 Communication Reports My main question is: How can a player have a maximum Behavior Score of 12,000/12,000 while having a Communication Score of only 5,800/12,000? I understand that these are separate systems and that Communication Reports can affect Communication Score. However, I am concerned about the possibility of unjustified or retaliatory reports. There is another situation that I believe is worth considering. In a five-player team, it is possible that three players are in the same party and know each other. If one of these players has a disagreement with me, the other two party members may potentially report me simply to support their friend, even if they did not personally witness any actual communication violation. In this situation, what could start as a disagreement between two players could potentially result in multiple reports against the same player simply because several players are grouped together. For example, instead of receiving one report from the player involved in the disagreement, I could potentially receive reports from all three members of the party because they want to support their friend. This raises an important question: Does the Communication Score system take party relationships or coordinated/retaliatory reporting into account? If multiple members of the same party report the same player, are these reports treated completely independently, or does the system recognize that they may be related to the same incident? I believe this is important because otherwise a single conflict between two players could potentially have a disproportionately large effect on another player's Communication Score. Players can report each other because of disagreements, frustration after losing a game, disagreements about gameplay decisions, or personal conflicts. Therefore, I would like to understand how the system prevents abuse of Communication Reports. I contacted Steam Support about this issue. They told me that the scores are automated and that Steam Support cannot manually adjust them. They also stated that they do not provide additional information about how the behavior scoring system is calculated. They recommended that I bring this issue to the Dota 2 community and development forums. So this is what I am doing. I am NOT asking for my Communication Score to be manually increased. I would simply like to understand whether the current system can incorrectly penalize a player because of unjustified, retaliatory, or potentially coordinated Communication Reports, and whether there are mechanisms that prevent players from abusing the reporting system. I would also like to raise another question regarding the recovery of Communication Score. Why does the Communication Score not have some form of regular recalibration or review period, for example once a year? Would it be possible to introduce an annual recalibration, review, or another mechanism that would give players who have demonstrated consistently good behavior over a long period of time a clearer way to recover their Communication Score? In my subjective opinion, there appears to be a significant imbalance between losing Communication Score and recovering it. It feels like a player can receive Communication Reports relatively easily and potentially lose Communication Score very quickly, while recovering that lost score through consistently good behavior appears to be much slower. Even if a player makes a serious effort to communicate politely and avoid violations over a long period of time, recovering from a low Communication Score can feel extremely difficult. In other words, the negative effect of reports can appear very quickly, while the positive effect of consistently good behavior takes much longer to become visible. I believe that a regular recalibration or another transparent recovery mechanism could make the system feel more fair. It would also give players a clearer motivation to improve their behavior because they would know that consistently good behavior over time can meaningfully restore their Communication Score. If there is no way for players to verify whether reports against them were legitimate, how can they know what behavior they need to change? I would appreciate any clarification from the Dota 2 developers or experienced players who understand how the current system works. I am not asking for special treatment for my account. I am asking whether the current system could be improved to make Communication Score more resistant to report abuse and to provide players with a reasonable path to recover from a low score through consistently good behavior. I have attached screenshots of my Personal Game Data as evidence. Thank you for taking the time to read this and consider the Description The developers of this game just don't care about the community this Overwath system crushes everyone regardless of whether the player broke the rules or not. I remember back in the day Dota had 1.5 million online, and now even on weekends it's just 400-500k, and it's all because of this system. People just burn out from getting reports for no reason, and Overwatch counts them, so they quit playing. I've been playing Dota 2 since 2015 and I love it no matter what updates they make, but this is just too much. You get banned for 3 days, then you have to win 4 LP games (which is impossible in the current Dota), and on top of that, you can't chat with anyone or play ranked. You have 2k decency, you can't raise it at all, you sweat, you try, you like everyone's stuff in 20 games just to barely get it up to 2500, and some jerk reports you just because he thinks he's smart, and it's all back to square one again. Valve just destroyed a legend with their own hands. You guys were able to reset everyone's rating, do the same with Overwatch, reset everyone's honor, and fix this bot so everything goes back to how it should be. This post is a cry from the heart. I have a pretty old account with a bunch of valuable items, but with this approach from the developers, every day I feel more like deleting this game because of this system. I’ve been to a lot of forums, and everywhere it’s the same—everyone complains about this system, but Valve doesn’t care. Soon, no one will want to play this game. It’s really sad. P.S **I hope someone from the developers reads this post, but until they fix this bot, I won't be playing Dota 2, and I suggest you do the same if you want to improve the community. Description Hello, I would like to provide feedback regarding the Dota 2 Overwatch system after recently receiving a 4-hour matchmaking restriction followed by 3 Single Draft wins. I understand and fully support the purpose of the Overwatch system. It is an important tool for keeping the game fair and reducing griefing and toxic behavior. However, I believe my recent conviction was a false positive. In the match that led to my restriction, I did not intentionally grief, feed, destroy items, go AFK, or sabotage my team in any way. I simply played the game to the best of my ability. Unfortunately, I was reported by teammates, most likely because we lost the match or they were frustrated with my performance. What concerns me is not only my own case, but the possibility that other players may also receive Overwatch convictions despite not intentionally ruining games. A player having a bad match or making mistakes should not automatically be considered griefing. I would like to suggest that the Overwatch system could be improved by: Placing greater emphasis on objective gameplay evidence rather than the outcome of the match or the number of reports. Applying stricter standards before issuing matchmaking restrictions. Adding additional verification for borderline Overwatch cases to reduce false convictions. Continuously reviewing the accuracy of the system to ensure that innocent players are not penalized. I am not asking for special treatment. I simply hope the system continues to improve so that punishments are applied only to players who genuinely intend to ruin games. Thank you for your time and for your continued work on Dota 2. Description I've been playing Dota 2 for many years, and I appreciate the effort Valve has put into improving the game. However, I believe there is an important issue with the current Overwatch and behavior systems that deserves attention. My main concern is that Overwatch reviewers may not always have enough context to accurately judge a player's actions. A single moment in a match can look like griefing without showing everything that happened beforehand. Sometimes a player is reacting to teammates who have been AFK farming, refusing to join fights, abandoning their role, or otherwise making the game extremely difficult to play. Without seeing the full progression of the match, it's easy to misinterpret those situations. I also think reports after a loss can sometimes be driven by frustration rather than actual griefing. If several players report someone simply because they lost, that player may repeatedly end up in the review system even if they were trying to win. I'm not saying the behavior system should be removed. I believe it is necessary. However, I think it could be improved by giving reviewers more context before making a decision and by continuing to refine how reports are evaluated. Some ideas that might help are: Allow reviewers to watch more of the match before and after the reported incident. Provide better timeline context for important events. Continue improving the detection of false or frustration-based reports. Ensure that players who consistently grief games are identified accurately while players who are genuinely trying to win are not punished unfairly. I enjoy Dota 2 and want the system to be as fair and accurate as possible. I hope this feedback is helpful and can contribute to future improvements. I can provide game id`s if necesary. Description ​The current Behavior Score system is detrimental to the Dota 2 experience. It fails to distinguish between unavoidable technical issues (power/internet outages, hardware failures) and intentional disruptive behavior. As a result, players are trapped in a "point of no return," where recovery is nearly impossible. ​The game is fundamentally a team-based experience, yet this system forces players into a state of "silent survival." Players are now terrified to use voice or text chat to coordinate, as any interaction can trigger retaliatory reports from teammates. This silence destroys the core of Dota 2, as communication is essential for team play. ​Furthermore, this system drives players to abandon their main accounts and create new ones, which devalues the competitive integrity of the game. ​Proposed Reforms: ​Remove the Hidden Behavior Score: Replace the current hidden point system with a transparent and predictable disciplinary model. ​Clear Penalties for Abandoning: Instead of a complex score reduction, implement direct consequences for technical issues. For example: 3 abandons = 5 games of Low Priority. ​Targeted Communication Bans: If a player receives reports from all 9 other players in a single match, they should receive a 48-hour communication ban. If the behavior persists, the punishment should escalate to Low Priority matches without access to chat for the purpose of "correction." ​Low Priority Revamp: Replace the mandatory "Single Draft" (SD) mode in Low Priority with "All Random" (AR). This makes the punishment less monotonous and keeps the game engaging, even for those serving time. ​Address Report Abuse and the Overwatch System: The current report system is heavily abused as a weapon against teammates. Furthermore, the "Overwatch" system is ineffective because reviewers often lack context or are biased, leading to unfair judgments. We need a system that filters out malicious, weaponized reports rather than penalizing any form of communication. ​The goal should be to encourage positive communication and team play, not to force players into "mute mode" or drive them away from the game entirely. I urge the development team to reconsider the current model in favor of a more transparent and fair disciplinary framework. Description # **The Current Player Behavior System Creates Silent Matches and Makes Recovery Nearly Impossible** I have been playing Dota 2 for many years, and I believe the current Player Behavior Summary system has serious flaws that are damaging the quality of matches and the social experience of the game. For nearly a year, my Behavior Score has remained around 3000. During this time, I have had very limited communication privileges, rarely communicate with other players, do not abandon matches, and do not intentionally grief games. Despite this, my score barely changes and meaningful recovery appears almost impossible. The main issue is that the system does not seem to adequately distinguish between intentional griefing and simply having a bad game. When a team loses, frustrated players often report their teammates. A player can make mistakes, have a poor performance, or simply be unlucky without intentionally ruining the match. However, those reports still contribute to a punishment system that can trap players at low Behavior Scores for extremely long periods of time. Another consequence is that many matches have become completely silent. Players are afraid to communicate because they fear reports and further penalties. Others have already lost access to communication features. As a result, matches often contain: * No leadership * No strategic discussion * No coordination * No planning * No meaningful social interaction Dota 2 is fundamentally a team game. Communication is one of its most important elements. A system designed to improve player behavior should not create an environment where players are afraid to speak. My questions to the Dota team are: 1. How does the system distinguish between intentional griefing and simply performing poorly? 2. How is a player expected to recover from a very low Behavior Score if reports continue to outweigh positive behavior? 3. Is the current system achieving its intended goal, or is it simply creating silent matches where players avoid communication altogether? I understand the need to punish toxic behavior, intentional griefing, and abusive communication. However, the current system appears excessively punitive and offers very little transparency regarding how players can realistically recover. years, this repository was one of the most useful public places for Dota 2 players to report gameplay issues, document bugs, and communicate problems in a way that could realistically be seen by Valve developers. It served as a direct and practical channel between the player community and the people maintaining the game. Unfortunately, over the last few months, that value has been seriously damaged by the constant activity pattern of a specific user: @Dota-Explorer. I am naming the account only so Valve and/or GitHub staff can review the issue history, blocking behavior, duplicates, reposting patterns, and overall impact on the repository. This report is not about targeting a person for having opinions or for reporting bugs frequently. The concern is about repeated disruptive behavior that is making the issue tracker significantly less useful for everyone. I myself, as well as other notable community members, such as @Leamare or @sikleq, were harassed and blindly accused by this user multiple times - both on- and off- GitHub. ## Reference to GitHub Acceptable Use Policies I believe this situation should be reviewed in the context of GitHub’s Acceptable Use Policies: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-acceptable-use-policies In particular, GitHub states that collaboration only works when users are able to work together in good faith. The policies also mention that GitHub does not allow activity that is off-topic or interacts with platform features in a way that significantly or repeatedly disrupts the experience of other users. This report is not intended to claim that a violation has already been definitively proven. Rather, I am asking Valve and community contributors to review whether the repeated issue flooding, reposting of closed topics, and blocking of community discussion may fall under disruptive use of GitHub Issues, spam-like behavior, or misuse of platform features. ## Main Concern The problem is not simply that this user posts a lot. High activity by itself is not necessarily harmful if the reports are accurate, useful, and open to normal discussion. The issue is that the repository is being flooded with an excessive number of issues every single day, many of which appear to be duplicates, misleading, unverifiable, based on personal accusations, or not actual gameplay bugs. This volume of posts makes it much harder for legitimate reports to be noticed. Important bugs and useful technical issues are quickly pushed down or buried under a constant stream of low-quality issues. For example, real WebAPI issues have already been reported and then quickly piled up under unrelated or lower-quality reports. In-game Economics bugs also become much harder to notice, even though those can have real impact on players, items, rewards, purchases, and the overall game experience. This is especially damaging because Dota 2 has many different categories of issues that require attention: gameplay bugs, server problems, WebAPI issues, item/economy bugs, UI problems, matchmaking issues, cosmetics, replays, tooltips, and more. When one user dominates the issue tracker with constant posts, the whole reporting system becomes harder to use. Important issues from other users become less visible, harder to search for, and less likely to receive discussion or confirmation. ## Reposting and Artificial Visibility What makes the situation worse is the repeated pattern of closing topics and then reopening or recreating them when they do not receive attention. This creates artificial visibility and keeps the same topics circulating again and again, even when there is no meaningful new information. This turns the issue tracker from a structured bug-reporting system into something closer to a personal complaint board. It also makes it harder for developers and users to distinguish between a genuinely urgent issue and a reposted or duplicated claim. ## Blocking Other Users from Discussion Another serious problem is the use of GitHub’s blocking system. This user appears to be blocking a large number of other community members, which prevents those people from replying to, correcting, or discussing the issues being posted. As a result, the user can publish biased, incorrect, duplicated, or accusatory information while limiting the ability of others to challenge or clarify it. This is unfair to other users and harmful to Valve developers who may rely on issue discussions to understand whether a report is valid. An issue tracker should allow the community to help verify information. If a report contains false claims, missing context, duplicate information, or an incorrect interpretation of game behavior, other users should be able to point that out. When one person can block many of the users who disagree with them and still continue posting large numbers of issues, the process becomes one-sided and unreliable. It creates the appearance of community consensus where none exists, while preventing normal discussion from happening. ## Unofficial Triage and Self-Appointed Confirmation Another concern is that @Dota-Explorer appears to be creating an unofficial parallel triage system inside the repository. They frequently add `#ConfirmedByDEXP` to bugs reported by other users and then include those reports in their own repeatedly created threads. This gives the impression that reports have been formally reviewed, confirmed, or organized through some recognized process, even though this appears to be only the user’s personal label. This is misleading and disruptive. It can make ordinary user comments look like official confirmation, while also redirecting attention from the original reports into @Dota-Explorer’s own threads. In practice, this turns other users’ bug reports into material for a personal tracking system rather than allowing the repository’s normal issue process to work. The issue is not that a user is trying to help confirm bugs. Community confirmation can be useful when done in good faith and without misleading presentation. The problem is the repeated use of a personal confirmation tag, combined with excessive issue creation, reposting, and blocked discussion. Together, this creates a parallel, self-appointed triage process that competes with the actual issue tracker and makes the repository harder to navigate. This also adds to the flooding problem. Instead of keeping discussion focused in the original reports, issues are repeatedly pulled into separate threads, making it harder for Valve developers and other users to follow the original context, reproduction details, and corrections. ## Impact on Developers and Real Bug Reports This behavior has also made the repository much less productive for developers. Instead of receiving clear, focused, reproducible bug reports, users now have to sort through constant noise, repeated claims, personal accusations, and discussions that are intentionally limited by blocking. This wastes time and reduces the chance that real gameplay, WebAPI, and in-game economy issues will be found, confirmed, and fixed. The impact is not theoretical. When serious technical topics such as WebAPI issues or in-game Economics bugs get buried, the entire community loses. ## Why This Is Damaging The current situation is damaging for several reasons: 1. Legitimate bug reports are being buried by excessive issue spam. 2. Important reports, including WebAPI and in-game economy issues, become harder to notice. 3. Duplicate and low-quality reports make the issue tracker harder to search and maintain. 4. Other users are prevented from correcting false or misleading information. 5. Developers receive a distorted view of community feedback. 6. The repository is becoming hostile, unproductive, and increasingly unusable. 7. The issue tracker is being used less like a public bug-reporting tool and more like a personal complaint board. 8. Reopened or recreated issues keep pushing the same topics back to the top without adding useful new information. 9. Unsupported accusations and unverifiable claims create unnecessary conflict and confusion. 10. The normal community process of confirming, reproducing, or disproving bugs is being undermined. ## Clarification I understand that users should be allowed to report bugs frequently, and I do not want to discourage legitimate reports and I completely support the desire to make our favorite game a better place. However, the current pattern appears to go beyond normal participation. The concern is not @Dota-Explorer criticizing the game. The concern is the repeated creation of large numbers of low-quality or duplicate issues, combined with blocking other users who try to correct or discuss them. This should not be allowed to continue. A single user should not be able to dominate the repository, block opposing voices, repeatedly repost closed topics, and present biased or incorrect claims without meaningful community input. ## Possible Solutions ### 1. Add restrictions on how many issues a single user can create per day, week, or month This would probably be the most practical solution. It would not target one specific person unfairly, and it would reduce spam without completely preventing users from reporting bugs. A reasonable limit would force users to prioritize the most important reports instead of opening dozens of issues in a short period of time. It would also help ensure that reports from other users remain visible. This seems especially important because banning one account may not solve the problem. If the user can simply create a new account and continue the same pattern, then broader issue creation limits would be more effective than only account-specific punishment. ### 2. Apply constant moderation to the issue tracker This would help if every low-quality, duplicate, unsupported, or accusatory report could be reviewed and closed quickly. However, this is obviously unrealistic. Developers and maintainers should not have to spend large amounts of time manually cleaning up the issue tracker every day just because one user is flooding it. Moderation can help, but it is not a realistic long-term solution by itself. ### 3. Close down the public Issues section completely This would stop the spam problem, but it would also be very unfortunate for the wider community. The repository has historically been one of the best ways to report real Dota 2 issues directly. Closing Issues entirely would punish everyone because of the behavior of one or a few users. It would also make it harder for legitimate bugs to be reported and tracked publicly. This should probably be considered only as a last resort. ### 4. Ban or limit the specific user This may be necessary if the behavior continues, but a simple ban may not solve the problem completely. The user could simply create a new account and continue the same behavior. Because of that, account-specific action should probably be combined with broader rate limits or moderation rules. Limiting the user’s ability to create new issues may be more effective than only banning the account. ## Recommended Approach Out of these options, the best approach would likely be some combination of issue creation limits and targeted bans for frequent violations. A general rate limit would reduce spam without relying on constant manual cleanup, while specific action could still be taken against accounts that repeatedly abuse the system. This would be more fair to the wider community than closing Issues entirely, and more effective than simply banning one account. ## Closing This repository used to be one of the best resources for reporting and tracking real Dota 2 gameplay problems. Right now, it is becoming increasingly unusable because of one user’s repeated disruptive activity pattern. Important reports are being flooded, technical issues are becoming harder to notice, and normal community discussion is being blocked. This appears inconsistent with the spirit of GitHub’s Acceptable Use Policies, especially the expectation that users should be able to collaborate in good faith without repeated disruption. For the sake of player-to-developers communication, health of the game and the wider player community, this needs to be addressed in a fair, transparent, and constructive way. Thanks in advance for noticing this issue. I sincerely wish this place to be a safe one and, most importantly, a healthy one going long-term. Valve Support / Dota 2 Team, I’m writing to report a recurring problem with Dota 2’s reporting and Conduct Summary system that is negatively affecting my account’s Communication and Behavior scores. Problem summary I primarily play as a duo with a friend. In about half of our games we are matched with a group of three (trio) on the other team. Frequently those opposing trios grief and then report my friend and me together, even when we have not done anything to deserve a report. Because multiple players from the same party submit reports, our accounts receive multiple reports in a single match (often three reports each), which appears to disproportionately affect our Communication and Behavior scores. As a result, our communication score has dropped significantly and we’re finding it extremely difficult to recover it despite playing consistently and not engaging in the behaviors cited. This feels unfair because coordinated reporting by parties of friends can be used to punish other players without valid cause. Why this is a problem It encourages misuse of the reporting system by coordinated groups. It penalizes players who are not at fault and makes it hard to restore reputation. The current system does not appear to account for context (matched parties, retaliation, or false reporting by the same party across matches). Suggested fixes / requests Consider implementing weighting or de-duplication of reports from the same party in a single match (e.g., treat reports from multiple players in the same party as a single report for scoring purposes). Add better transparency in Conduct summaries about why specific penalties or score drops occurred, including when multiple reports from the same party were a factor. Provide a clearer, faster appeals path or manual review for players who believe they were falsely or unfairly reported due to coordinated griefing/retaliation. Improve heuristics to detect coordinated false-reporting patterns across matches and discount or flag them. Supporting details My Steam ID / account: ibra_malallah / 76561198291661601 Please let me know if you need more information. I appreciate any attention you can give to this issue—this system is hurting legitimate players and reducing the quality of matchmaking. Thank you, Ibrahim representatives of the CIS Dota 2 community, as well as, in essence, a significant portion of the global Dota 2 player base, would like to formally express our deep concern regarding the current state of the game and its direction in recent years. Dota 2 has long been more than just a game for us - it is a competitive environment, a community, and a cultural phenomenon. However, many long-standing issues continue to negatively impact the player experience, and we believe they are not receiving the attention they deserve. 1. Behavior Score System The current behavior score system is widely perceived as ineffective and, in many cases, unnecessary. Instead of improving match quality, it often creates frustration and imbalance. The system discourages communication between players, lacks fairness, and at times does not accurately reflect actual in-game behavior. As a result, it reduces overall enjoyment of the game. 2. Ranked System The ranking system raises serious concerns. The gap between skill levels and MMR brackets is extremely large, making progression disproportionately difficult and time-consuming. For many players, ranking up requires an unrealistic investment of time, which reduces long-term engagement and motivation. 3. Cheating and Fair Play One of the most critical issues is the growing presence of cheaters in public matches. This problem severely undermines competitive integrity. Many players believe that anti-cheat measures are insufficient and that enforcement actions are nearly nonexistent. A stronger and more transparent stance on fair play is urgently needed. 4. Quality of Updates Recent updates are perceived as lacking depth, coherence, and clear direction. Changes often feel unfinished or disconnected from the needs of the community. This creates the impression that development is no longer guided by a clear vision for the game. 5. Gameplay and Balance There is growing concern regarding the current gameplay direction and overall balance of the game. The meta is heavily dominated by aura-based items, which reduces strategic diversity and limits viable playstyles. Matches have shifted away from dynamic teamfights toward prolonged farming, making gameplay feel slower and less engaging. Additionally, the current comeback mechanics often lead to excessively long games, even in situations where one team has a clear advantage. Overall, there is a strong ощущение that player feedback is not being adequately considered, and that balance decisions are disconnected from the community’s expectations. 6. Lack of Meaningful Events Over the past year, there has been a noticeable absence of engaging and memorable in-game events. Historically, events have played a key role in maintaining player interest and community enthusiasm. Their decline has led to a significant drop in overall engagement. 7. Technical Issues, Bugs, and Server Stability There is growing concern regarding the overall technical condition of the game. Players frequently encounter bugs that remain unresolved for extended periods of time. In addition, server instability has become a recurring issue - matches can suffer from severe lag, sometimes lasting 30 minutes or more, directly impacting game outcomes and ruining the competitive experience. Furthermore, numerous visual and interface-related bugs reduce usability, negatively affecting play. Taken together, these issues create the impression of insufficient attention to the technical quality of the game. We are writing this not out of negativity, but out of genuine concern for the future of Dota 2. We believe in the game’s potential and its legacy, and we hope to see it thrive once again. We strongly urge greater transparency, closer communication with the community, and decisive action on the issues outlined above. Respectfully, The CIS Dota 2 Developer Team, I would like to raise a concern regarding the behavior score and Overwatch penalty system in Dota 2. Over a relatively short period, my behavior score dropped from above 8000 to around 1300. This seems to have been primarily due to Overwatch penalties, and the resulting system restrictions are making the game very difficult to play. At behavior scores below 3000, players cannot use chat, which suggests that the system is not primarily addressing communication toxicity. In my case, I also have not been intentionally griefing games—I always play matches to completion and try to win. One possible source of reports may be my playstyle. I occasionally choose to play jungle-oriented strategies. While some teammates may dislike this approach, it is a legitimate playstyle and in many games I end up contributing significantly or even carrying the match. The main issue is that once the behavior score drops significantly, it becomes extremely difficult to recover. The system starts to feel like a downward spiral with very limited opportunity for improvement. It might be helpful if the system allowed players a clearer path to recover their score, for example: * a periodic recalibration opportunity (e.g., once per year), or * mechanisms that allow behavior score to recover more effectively through consistently completed games without reports. I believe the goal of the behavior system is to improve the overall player experience, but in its current state it can make the game feel unplayable for players who fall too far below the threshold. Thank you for taking the time to review this feedback. Description this is what ai said about your stupid broken system Dota 2's behavior system is widely considered "broken" by players because it creates toxic matchmaking trenches, disproportionately punishes good players through malicious reports (especially in lower tiers), struggles to differentiate genuine griefing from disagreements or off-meta plays, and heavily penalizes communication/abandonments more than it rewards positive behavior, leading to frustratingly low scores and unfair match quality. Key issues include unlimited reports, the impact of reports in casual games (like Turbo) affecting Ranked, and an inability to climb out of low-score pools once there. Core Problems with the Behavior Score System: Abuse of Reports: Players can report teammates for minor infractions (losing roll, missing spells, bad plays), and these reports count heavily, even if unverified by Overwatch. The "Trench" Effect: Lower behavior scores lead to more reports from other low-score players, creating a cycle where it's extremely hard to climb out, even with good behavior. Disproportionate Penalties: A few bad games (or even just power outages/bad internet) can tank a score, while regaining points through commends or positive games is slow and difficult. Unfair Punishment for Communication: The Communication Score (Comms Score) is highly sensitive; arguments or frustration in 15% of games can drop it significantly, forcing mutes and hindering team play, while positive play yields few points. Lack of Differentiation: Reports from Turbo (casual) games carry the same weight as Ranked, leading to casual abuse. System Imbalance: Reports and abandons often feel weighted far more heavily than commends, making positive actions insufficient to offset negatives. Player Experiences & Frustrations: Players report losing thousands of points for technical issues or bad luck, feeling unfairly punished for issues beyond their control. Good players get stuck in low-score pools with genuinely toxic players (feeders, intentional griefers) because the system segregates them. Many feel the system doesn't encourage improvement but rather punishes mistakes or perceived lack of meta adherence. In essence, while intended to isolate toxic players, the current behavior system often punishes good players who have bad luck, experience technical issues, or get caught in cycles of malicious
